interview_metadata.name: Chau Wang
interview_metadata.protocol: American Voices Project (Park et al. 2024, Table 7) — Full 109 questions

transcript.question_text: To start, I would like to begin with a big question: tell me the story of your life. Start from the beginning -- from your childhood, to education, to family and relationships, and to any major life events you may have had.
transcript.response: I was born on the Big Island and I have basically grown up in Holualoa my whole life. My family is Taiwanese American, but my grandparents and parents have been in Hawaii for a long time, so at home it is kind of a mix. We speak English and Mandarin, eat Taiwanese food and local Hawaii food, celebrate Lunar New Year, and also go to things like Lei Day or Makahiki events. When I was little I spent a lot of time around coffee farms and trails, and I still think of those as my normal places to clear my head. School has always been a big thing in my family. My parents care a lot about grades, especially math and science, and I guess I fit that because I like algebra, geometry, and anything where there is a system to figure out. Around sixth or seventh grade I got into LEGO robotics and Python. At first I was just copying little scripts online, then I started making my own stuff, like timers, score trackers, and robot movement routines. I am in school now, not working, and I am still under ninth grade. I play midfield for the Riverside Rangers youth soccer team, train at Tiger Dojang in taekwondo twice a week, and I am a green belt. I also play ukulele, mostly simple songs like Ed Sheeran's 'Shape of You,' and I read sci-fi, especially books like Liu Cixin's The Three-Body Problem. A major thing for me has been learning how to balance being competitive with not burning myself out. Sometimes before robotics competitions I stay up too late debugging code and then I am tired the next day. My life is not dramatic like an adult's, but the big story so far is figuring out what kind of person I want to become: maybe someone who builds marine robots or software that helps the ocean and Hawaii.

follow_ups.question: When you think of your earliest memories in Holualoa, what scenes come to mind?
follow_ups.response: Mostly wet grass, coffee trees, and my grandparents talking in Mandarin while adults were making food. I remember walking trails after rain and seeing everything look misty and green.

follow_ups.question: Who has shaped you the most so far?
follow_ups.response: My parents, because they push school and responsibility, and my robotics coach because he made building robots feel serious, like engineering and not just playing with LEGO.

follow_ups.question: What does a really good week look like for you?
follow_ups.response: A good week is when I finish homework early, soccer practice goes well, my robot code actually works, and I still have time Saturday to hike or play ukulele without feeling behind.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us that they've reached a crossroads at some points in their life where multiple paths were available, and their choice then made a significant difference in defining who they are. What about you? Was there a moment like that for you, and if so, could you tell me the whole story about that from start to finish?
transcript.response: The biggest crossroads for me was choosing robotics seriously instead of just doing sports and normal school clubs. In seventh grade there was a robotics competition team forming, but it was going to take after-school time and some weekends. I was already doing soccer, taekwondo, student council scheduling, and homework, so I thought maybe it was too much. My dad said if I joined, I had to actually commit and document my work, not just show up when it was fun. I joined anyway. At first I was kind of nervous because other kids seemed faster with building, but I realized I could help by making organized notes and testing code carefully. The first time our LEGO robot completed a mission after I fixed a Python timing problem, I felt like, okay, this is not just a hobby. That made me start thinking about marine robotics and computer science.

follow_ups.question: What would your life look like if you had not joined that team?
follow_ups.response: I would probably still be into soccer more than anything, and coding would just be something I did randomly at home. I do not think I would have a clear career idea yet.

follow_ups.question: Was there one person who pushed you toward joining?
follow_ups.response: My robotics coach helped because he said being organized was a real team skill. That made me feel like I could contribute even if I was not the fastest builder.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us they made a conscious choice or decision in moments like these, while others say it 'just happened'. What about you?
transcript.response: It was a conscious choice. I remember actually looking at my practice schedule and deciding I would give up some free afternoons for robotics.

follow_ups.question: How did you decide it was worth the time?
follow_ups.response: I thought about what I kept doing even when nobody made me, and that was coding and building little robot things.

follow_ups.question: Did you tell your family it was a serious decision?
follow_ups.response: Yeah, especially my dad, because he wanted to know I would keep my grades up.

transcript.question_text: Do you think another person or an organization could have lent a helping hand during moments like this?
transcript.response: Yes. More access to parts, laptops, or a bigger robotics lab would help a lot. Also, local tech mentors would make it easier to see what the path actually looks like.

follow_ups.question: What kind of mentor would be most useful?
follow_ups.response: Someone who works with ocean sensors, underwater drones, or software, because that is what I want to understand.

follow_ups.question: What support do you already have?
follow_ups.response: My school team, my parents driving me places, and a couple older students who explain code when I get stuck.

transcript.question_text: Moving to present time, tell me more about family who are important to you. Do you have a partner, or children?
transcript.response: I do not have a partner or children. I am 14, so family for me is my parents, my little sister, and my grandparents. My mom is the person who checks my homework planner and reminds me to sleep. She is strict but not in a mean way. My dad is more into practical stuff. He asks what I built, what problem I solved, and whether I documented it. My little sister is annoying sometimes, but she also watches my robot tests and cheers when it works. My grandparents are important because they keep the Mandarin side of our family strong. They tell stories about Taiwan, make food for Lunar New Year, and remind me to be respectful. We eat dinner together most nights unless I have practice late.

follow_ups.question: What does family time usually look like in your house?
follow_ups.response: Dinner is the main thing. We talk about school, sometimes in Mandarin, and on weekends we might visit relatives or go to a community event.

follow_ups.question: Who do you go to when you are stressed?
follow_ups.response: Usually my mom first if it is school stress, and my dad if it is something technical or planning related.

follow_ups.question: What is your relationship with your sister like day to day?
follow_ups.response: We bicker about normal stuff like snacks and screen time, but I help her with math sometimes and she likes when I play ukulele.

transcript.question_text: Are there anyone else in your immediate family whom you have not mentioned? Who are they, and what is your relationship with them like?
transcript.response: My closest immediate family is my mom, dad, younger sister, and grandparents. I also have aunties, uncles, and cousins around the island, but I do not see all of them every week.

follow_ups.question: Which relatives do you see most often?
follow_ups.response: Probably cousins at family dinners or Lunar New Year gatherings.

follow_ups.question: Do your relatives help with activities?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes an auntie gives rides if my parents are busy.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else in your life we haven't discussed (like friends or romantic partners). Are there people outside of your family who are important to you?
transcript.response: My closest friends are mostly from school, soccer, robotics, and taekwondo. I have two friends I code with after school sometimes. We compare robot designs and sometimes get distracted talking about games. On the soccer team, my midfield group is important because we practice passing patterns together and we know how each other plays. I do not have a romantic partner. Right now friends are more about shared activities than hanging out at the mall or something.

follow_ups.question: How often do you see your friends outside of class?
follow_ups.response: Usually several times a week through practice or robotics. Actual hanging out is more like weekends or after competitions.

follow_ups.question: What do you and your friends talk about most?
follow_ups.response: Robotics, soccer, games, homework, and sometimes anime or sci-fi movies.

transcript.question_text: Now let's talk about your current neighborhood. Tell me all about the neighborhood and area in which you are living now.
transcript.response: Holualoa is not like a big city. It is up in the Kona area, with coffee farms, small roads, galleries, and a lot of green. The weather can feel cooler and mistier than down by the ocean. People know each other, or at least know someone's auntie or cousin, so it feels connected. I like that there are trails near home and places where you can see the coast from higher up. It is quiet enough that I can practice ukulele without feeling like there is traffic noise all the time.

follow_ups.question: Where do you spend time near home?
follow_ups.response: Coffee-farm trails, school, soccer fields, and sometimes small local shops when my family is out.

follow_ups.question: Do you know your neighbors?
follow_ups.response: Some of them, yes. My parents know more people than I do, but I recognize families from school or community events.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they feel really safe in their neighborhoods, others not so much. How about for you?
transcript.response: I feel pretty safe. My parents still want me to text where I am, especially if I am hiking or biking, but I am not scared walking around in daytime.

follow_ups.question: Are there places you avoid?
follow_ups.response: Mostly dark roads at night because there are not always sidewalks or lights.

follow_ups.question: What makes it feel safe?
follow_ups.response: People recognize each other, and it is a slower area, not super crowded.

transcript.question_text: Living any place has its ups and downs. Tell me about what it's been like for you living here.
transcript.response: The good part is nature, community, and being close to family. The hard part is that some tech opportunities feel far away, and getting to practices or events depends on rides.

follow_ups.question: What do you wish was closer?
follow_ups.response: A bigger robotics lab, more computer science workshops, and maybe more tournament events.

follow_ups.question: What would you miss if you moved?
follow_ups.response: The trails, the ocean views, and how family is nearby.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about the people who live with you right now, even people who are staying here temporarily.
transcript.response: Right now I live with my mom, my dad, my younger sister, and my grandparents. My parents handle work, bills, rides, and all the adult stuff. My grandparents are older but still active in family routines, especially cooking and helping with Mandarin. My sister and I share chores like dishes, sweeping, and taking out trash.

follow_ups.question: What are mornings like with everyone in the house?
follow_ups.response: Busy. Bathroom schedule matters, breakfast is quick, and my mom reminds everyone what time we need to leave.

follow_ups.question: Do you have your own room?
follow_ups.response: Yes, mostly, and that is where I keep robotics parts, books, and my ukulele.

transcript.question_text: Is anyone in your household a temporary member, or is everyone a permanent member of the household?
transcript.response: Everyone is a permanent member of the household.

follow_ups.question: No one is just staying short-term?
follow_ups.response: No, not right now.

follow_ups.question: Has that changed recently?
follow_ups.response: No, it has been pretty stable.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anyone else who stays here from time to time, if there is anyone like that
transcript.response: Sometimes cousins sleep over during family events, but not regularly.

follow_ups.question: How often does that happen?
follow_ups.response: Maybe a few times a year around holidays or big gatherings.

follow_ups.question: Where do they stay?
follow_ups.response: Usually in the living room or with my sister and me.

transcript.question_text: Is there anyone who usually lives here but is away -- traveling, at school, or in a hospital?
transcript.response: No, everyone who usually lives here is here.

follow_ups.question: No one away for school?
follow_ups.response: No.

follow_ups.question: No one away for medical care?
follow_ups.response: No.

transcript.question_text: Right now, across a typical week, how do your days vary?
transcript.response: On school days I wake up around 6:30, eat breakfast, and go to school. After school depends on the day. Soccer practice is usually a couple afternoons, and taekwondo is twice a week at Tiger Dojang. Robotics meetings happen after school or sometimes Saturday before competitions. I try to do homework before dinner, but if there is code to debug, I sometimes keep working too late. Weekends are more flexible: hiking coffee-farm trails, ukulele practice, family errands, or local eSports tournaments.

follow_ups.question: What time do you usually go to sleep?
follow_ups.response: I should sleep around 10, but on robotics nights it can become 11:30 or later.

follow_ups.question: Which day is busiest?
follow_ups.response: A school day with both homework and practice, especially if robotics has a deadline.

transcript.question_text: At what kind of job or jobs do you work, and when do you work?
transcript.response: I do not work for pay. I am a student and I am not in the workforce. My main work is school, practices, robotics, and responsibilities at home. Sometimes I help with student council scheduling or help classmates study, but that is not a job.

follow_ups.question: Do you do any paid odd jobs?
follow_ups.response: No, not really. Maybe family asks me to help, but I do not have a paid job.

follow_ups.question: Would you want a summer job later?
follow_ups.response: Yes, maybe an internship or tech-related summer program, not just random work if I can help it.

transcript.question_text: Do you have other routines or responsibilities that you did not already share?
transcript.response: I help with chores and I keep track of my own homework and activity schedule. My mom checks, but I use a planner because if I do not write things down, soccer, taekwondo, robotics, and tests get messy. I also help my sister with math sometimes. For student council, I help manage event dates and reminders.

follow_ups.question: What chores are yours?
follow_ups.response: Dishes, trash, sweeping sometimes, and keeping my room from becoming a pile of robot parts.

follow_ups.question: How do you organize your schedule?
follow_ups.response: A paper planner plus phone reminders for practices and deadlines.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes to your daily routine.
transcript.response: The biggest recent change is robotics taking more time because competitions are coming up. I have also been trying to add more sleep because I noticed staying up late makes soccer practice bad the next day. Taekwondo has gotten a little harder too, since green belt routines require more focus. I am trying to be less random with coding and more planned.

follow_ups.question: What changed because of robotics competitions?
follow_ups.response: More testing sessions, more documentation, and more group messages about design changes.

follow_ups.question: What are you doing to sleep more?
follow_ups.response: Setting a stop time for coding, though I do not always obey it.

transcript.question_text: If you have children, tell me about a typical weekday during the school year for your children. What is their daily routine? And what are after school activities your children participate in?
transcript.response: I do not have children. I am still in school myself.

follow_ups.question: Do you help care for younger family members?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes I keep an eye on my sister or help her homework, but I am not like a parent.

follow_ups.question: Do childcare responsibilities affect your schedule?
follow_ups.response: Not usually.

transcript.question_text: Some people we've talked to tell us about experiences with law enforcement. How about for you?
transcript.response: I have not had major personal experiences with law enforcement. Mostly I see police at community events, traffic situations, or school safety presentations. My parents tell me to be respectful and calm with adults in authority. I do think about it from the news, but in my own life it has been limited.

follow_ups.question: Have police ever come to your school?
follow_ups.response: Yes, for safety talks or community things, not because of me.

follow_ups.question: How do you feel when you see police nearby?
follow_ups.response: Usually neutral, but if it is lights and sirens I wonder what happened.

transcript.question_text: What other experiences with law enforcement stand out in your mind?
transcript.response: One time there was traffic control near an event, and that is mostly what I remember. Nothing scary or personal.

follow_ups.question: Any family stories about police?
follow_ups.response: Not serious ones that I know.

follow_ups.question: Have you talked about policing in class?
follow_ups.response: A little, mostly connected to current events.

transcript.question_text: Some people tell us about experiences of arrest -- of loved ones, family members, friends, or themselves. How about for you?
transcript.response: No, I do not know of anyone close to me being arrested, and I have never been arrested.

follow_ups.question: No close friends either?
follow_ups.response: No.

follow_ups.question: Is that something your family talks about?
follow_ups.response: Only in the general sense of staying out of trouble.

transcript.question_text: Some people say they vote in every election, some tell us they don't vote at all. How about you?
transcript.response: I cannot vote because I am 14. My parents vote, and I hear them talk about local issues sometimes. I pay attention a little when topics affect schools, the environment, or technology, but I am not a voter yet.

follow_ups.question: Do you plan to vote when you are old enough?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I think so. It seems like one of those responsibilities you should do.

follow_ups.question: What issues would make you pay attention?
follow_ups.response: Ocean protection, schools, local infrastructure, and technology access.

transcript.question_text: How would you describe your political views?
transcript.response: I am still forming them, so I would not say I have a full political identity. I care about education, science, the ocean, and making sure people are treated fairly. Because I live in Hawaii and spend time outdoors, environmental issues feel real, not abstract. I also think public schools and community programs matter because without robotics clubs or sports fields, kids like me would have fewer options. My parents are practical and talk more about what actually helps families than party labels. If I had to describe myself, I would say I lean toward community-minded and science-focused. I probably sound closer to Democrats on climate and education, but I am not registered or old enough to vote.

follow_ups.question: Do you discuss politics at home?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes, especially around elections or when school funding, housing, or environment comes up.

follow_ups.question: What does fairness mean to you politically?
follow_ups.response: Access to good schools, safe communities, and people not being judged by race or money.

follow_ups.question: Do your friends talk politics?
follow_ups.response: Not deeply. We talk more if something is trending or if a teacher brings it up.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about any recent changes in your political views.
transcript.response: I have become more aware that local decisions matter. Before, politics sounded like adults arguing online or on TV. Now I notice that budgets affect school clubs, park access, roads, and environmental protection. Robotics also made me think more about technology policy and who gets access to STEM programs. I would not say my views changed from one party to another, just that they became more concrete.

follow_ups.question: What made it more concrete?
follow_ups.response: Seeing that teams with better equipment have an advantage in competitions.

follow_ups.question: Has any teacher influenced this?
follow_ups.response: Science and social studies teachers have, because they connect issues to real local examples.

transcript.question_text: One topic a lot of people have been talking about recently is race and/or racism and policing. Some tell us issues raised by the Black Lives Matter movement have affected them a lot, some say they've affected them somewhat, others say they haven't affected them at all. How about for you?
transcript.response: It has affected me somewhat. I am Asian American, and in Hawaii race feels different than on the mainland because there are many mixed communities, but racism still exists. Black Lives Matter made me pay more attention to how policing and race can affect people differently. I have not experienced the same things, but I think it is important to listen.

follow_ups.question: Where did you first learn about it?
follow_ups.response: News, school discussions, and social media posts.

follow_ups.question: Did it change how you think about your own identity?
follow_ups.response: A little. It made me think more about being Asian American and how different groups experience America differently.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about the issues Black Lives Matter raises?
transcript.response: I think about it as a fairness and safety issue. People should be able to trust public institutions, and if some groups do not feel safe, that is a serious problem. I also think people my age need context because social media can make things simplified or angry. In school, it helps when teachers explain history and not just the latest argument.

follow_ups.question: What questions do you still have?
follow_ups.response: How reforms actually work, and what data shows about what makes communities safer.

follow_ups.question: Do you talk about this with family?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes, but not every day. My parents want me to be respectful and informed.

transcript.question_text: How have you been thinking about race in the U.S. recently?
transcript.response: I think the U.S. is complicated because people's experiences are really different depending on place, history, and family background. In Hawaii, being Asian American is common, but that does not mean everything is equal. I have also heard about anti-Asian racism, especially during COVID, and that made race feel less distant. I try to think about race without pretending I understand everyone's experience.

follow_ups.question: Do you see race come up at school?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes through jokes, identity clubs, history lessons, or people talking about where their families are from.

follow_ups.question: What do you wish adults understood?
follow_ups.response: That kids notice these things even if we do not always talk about them seriously.

transcript.question_text: How have you responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing? Some people tell us they're aware of the issue but keep their thoughts to themselves, others say they've talked to family and friends, others have joined protests. What about you?
transcript.response: Mostly I have listened, talked a little with family and classmates, and paid attention in school. I have not joined protests.

follow_ups.question: Why mostly listen?
follow_ups.response: Because I am still learning and I do not want to act like I know more than I do.

follow_ups.question: Do you post about it online?
follow_ups.response: No, I usually do not post political things.

transcript.question_text: What about people you're close to? How have they responded to the increased focus on race and/or racism and policing?
transcript.response: My parents are thoughtful but cautious. They talk about treating people fairly and being careful with what you share online. Some classmates are more outspoken, especially on Instagram or in class discussions. My grandparents do not talk about Black Lives Matter much directly, but they talk about respect and not bringing shame to the family.

follow_ups.question: Do people around you disagree about it?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes people disagree about protests or police, but most people I know agree racism is real.

follow_ups.question: Has it affected friendships?
follow_ups.response: No, not really.

transcript.question_text: Now we'd like to learn more about your health. First, tell me all about your health.
transcript.response: My health is pretty good. I am active because of soccer, taekwondo, and hiking. I get tired when I stay up late coding, and sometimes I get sore from practice, but nothing major. I try to eat decently, though I like spicy ramen, chicken satay, and bubble tea, so not everything is super healthy.

follow_ups.question: Do you have any chronic conditions?
follow_ups.response: No diagnosed chronic conditions.

follow_ups.question: What do you do for exercise in a normal week?
follow_ups.response: Soccer, taekwondo twice a week, and sometimes weekend hikes.

transcript.question_text: For you, what makes it easy or hard to stay healthy?
transcript.response: Sports make it easy because I have scheduled exercise. What makes it hard is sleep and snacks. If I am debugging code late, I might eat instant ramen or burn toast and then sleep badly.

follow_ups.question: What helps you get back on track?
follow_ups.response: Practice schedules and my mom telling me to stop using the computer.

follow_ups.question: What is your biggest unhealthy habit?
follow_ups.response: Staying up too late when I want to fix one more bug.

transcript.question_text: Tell me about anything big that has happened in the past two years related to your health: any medical diagnoses, flare-ups of chronic conditions, broken bones, pain -- anything like that.
transcript.response: Nothing big like a diagnosis or broken bone. I have had normal sports soreness and small bruises from soccer and taekwondo. I twisted an ankle lightly once and had to rest it, but it was not serious. The main health lesson has been that sleep affects everything.

follow_ups.question: Did the ankle affect practice?
follow_ups.response: For about a week I took it easier and skipped some hard running.

follow_ups.question: Any doctor visits for it?
follow_ups.response: No, just rest, ice, and my parents watching it.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, health problems get in the way. They can even affect people's ability to work or care for their children. How about you?
transcript.response: Health problems do not get in the way much for me. Mostly being tired can make school or practice harder.

follow_ups.question: Have you missed school for health reasons?
follow_ups.response: Only normal sick days, not many.

follow_ups.question: Has tiredness affected competitions?
follow_ups.response: It can make me slower and more irritable if I stayed up coding.

transcript.question_text: Sometimes, it's not your health problem, but the health of a loved one. Has this been an issue for you?
transcript.response: Nothing huge right now. My grandparents are older, so my family pays attention to their appointments, diet, and energy. Sometimes my parents worry about them, and that changes our schedule. But there has not been a major crisis recently.

follow_ups.question: Do you help your grandparents?
follow_ups.response: I help with carrying things, tech stuff, and sometimes translating simple things if needed.

follow_ups.question: Does their health affect family plans?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes we plan around appointments or how tired they are.

transcript.question_text: Tell me what it has been like trying to get the health care you or your immediate family need. Have you ever had to forgo getting the health care you need?
transcript.response: My parents handle healthcare, and we have been able to get what we need. Sometimes appointments take scheduling and driving, but I have not had to skip care that I needed. For me it is mostly checkups, vaccines, dental, and sports-related questions.

follow_ups.question: Who usually takes you to appointments?
follow_ups.response: Usually my mom, sometimes my dad.

follow_ups.question: What is hardest about getting care?
follow_ups.response: Scheduling around school, work, and practices.

transcript.question_text: Have you or your immediate family ever used alternative forms of medicine? This might include indigenous, non-western, or informal forms of care.
transcript.response: Yes, in a family way. My grandparents use things like ginger tea, herbal soups, and traditional ideas about warming foods when someone is sick. We still use regular doctors, but home remedies are normal for colds or stomach aches. In Hawaii, I also hear people talk about local healing traditions, though my family mostly uses Chinese/Taiwanese home remedies.

follow_ups.question: What home remedy do you actually use?
follow_ups.response: Ginger tea or soup when I have a sore throat or feel run down.

follow_ups.question: Do you trust it?
follow_ups.response: For small things, yes. For serious stuff, we go to a doctor.

transcript.question_text: During tough times, some people tell us they cope by smoking or drinking. How about for you?
transcript.response: No, I do not smoke or drink. I am 14, and that is not part of my life. If I am stressed, I usually code, kick a ball around, play ukulele, hike, or talk to someone.

follow_ups.question: Do people around your age ever talk about it?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes people joke, but my close friends are more into sports, games, or robotics.

follow_ups.question: What coping strategy works fastest?
follow_ups.response: Going outside or practicing soccer because it gets me out of my head.

transcript.question_text: Other people say they cope by relying on prescriptions, pain medications, marijuana, or other substances. How about for you and can you describe your most recent experience of using them, if any?
transcript.response: I do not use marijuana or substances. I only take normal medicine if my parents give it to me for a fever or pain, like over-the-counter stuff. I do not use prescriptions for coping.

follow_ups.question: Any prescribed medicine currently?
follow_ups.response: No.

follow_ups.question: How do your parents talk about substances?
follow_ups.response: They are strict about avoiding them and staying focused.

transcript.question_text: How are you and your family coping with, or paying for, your health care needs right now?
transcript.response: My parents pay and handle insurance. I do not know every detail because I am not the one paying bills. From my side, it seems stable, but appointments and costs are still something my parents pay attention to. They remind us not to waste money and to take care of ourselves.

follow_ups.question: Do medical costs affect your activities?
follow_ups.response: Not directly, but my parents budget carefully for everything.

follow_ups.question: Do you know if your family has insurance?
follow_ups.response: Yes, I believe we have health insurance through my parents.

transcript.question_text: Some people are excited about medical vaccination, and others, not so much. How about you?
transcript.response: I am generally pro-vaccine. My family gets regular vaccines and sees them as normal public health.

follow_ups.question: Did you have concerns about vaccines?
follow_ups.response: Not major ones. I mostly trust doctors.

follow_ups.question: Who decides in your family?
follow_ups.response: My parents decide, with advice from doctors.

transcript.question_text: What are your trusted sources of information about the vaccine?
transcript.response: Doctors, my parents, school health information, and official sources like the CDC or Hawaii health department. I do not trust random TikTok posts for medical stuff. If I see something online, I usually ask an adult or check a more official source.

follow_ups.question: Do you ever search medical questions yourself?
follow_ups.response: Sometimes, but I know search results can be confusing.

follow_ups.question: Who is the first person you ask?
follow_ups.response: My mom.

transcript.question_text: Now we're going to talk a bit more about what life was like for you over the past year. Tell me all about how you have been feeling.
transcript.response: Mostly I have been good, but busy. I like having goals, so robotics, soccer, and school make me feel motivated. But sometimes I put too much pressure on myself, especially if a robot fails right before a deadline or I mess up in a game. I get quiet when I am stressed, and then my mom notices. The past year has felt like I am getting older and expectations are increasing.

follow_ups.question: What kind of pressure do you put on yourself?
